newsitem.title: USA: Lawmakers seek House vote on U.S. sugar program.
newsitem.headline: Lawmakers seek House vote on U.S. sugar program.

text.p: The controversial U.S. sugar program will come under attack again this week when House lawmakers take up the fiscal 1998 Agriculture Department spending bill, but it may not suffer any damage.
"We're definitely going to offer something," said Stephanie Elrod, a spokeswoman for Rep. Dan Miller, a Florida Republican who is one of the House's most ardent sugar program opponents.
But as of mid-day on Tuesday, Miller was still deciding between two different amendments -- both of which would change the U.S. price support loan program, she said.
One option would alter the "non-recourse" aspect of the sugar loan program, while the other would reduce the loan rate by five percent, Elrod said.
"We don't quite have the language hammered out," she said.
Jack Roney, director of economics at the American Sugar Alliance, said his group expects Miller to offer an amendment to eliminate non-recourse loans under the sugar program.
But ASA is also optimistic that it has rallied enough support in the House to prevent any change.
Eliminating non-recourse loans could jeopardize the price support function of the sugar program, Roney said.

Currently, whenever U.S. sugar imports are more than 1.5 million short tons annually, cane processors and beet sugar refiners have the option of forfeiting sugar stocks to the government rather than repaying USDA "non-recourse" loans.
That tends to support market prices at the loan level, which is 18 cents per pound for raw cane sugar and 22.9 cents per pound for refined beet sugar.
Replacing non-recourse loans with recourse loan would prevent processors and refiners from forfeiting stocks, thus making it more likely for sugar prices to fall below the loan-rate level.
USDA could still support U.S. sugar prices by restricting the amount of sugar entering the United States under the annual import quota.
But sugar producers are concerned future USDA officials might be more sympathetic to sugar users than to farmers and allow price-depressing amounts of imports, Roney said.

Miller and Rep. Charles Schumer, D-New York, put U.S. sugar producers on notice earlier this year that they planned to again go after the sugar program, which Congress reformed in the 1996 farm bill to make it more market oriented.
That has given the ASA plenty of time of to make its case to lawmakers for keeping the current program intact.
"We're optimistic that the Congress will stand by the committment it made in the 1996 farm bill" and not make any changes to the U.S. sugar program, Roney said.
